sections.text:
Solomon has finished praying, and fire comes down from heaven. It consumes the offering, and “the LORD’s glory filled the house.” So this book begins with Solomon and the building of the temple.

It then follows the kings of Judah alone, until the exile. The northern kingdom is mentioned only where it touches Judah’s story.

Again and again the book shows the same thing: when a king seeks God, humbles himself and prays, God answers and restores. It ends with a decree from Cyrus of Persia, who allows the exiles to go home and rebuild the temple. He says of any of God’s people, “let him go up”. The last word of the book is an open door, and it points toward home.

The book continues 1 Chronicles and was written after the exile. In the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles stands last among the books, so that the Scriptures end with the invitation to go up to Jerusalem, as the decree of Cyrus does.

The promise of 7:14, that God will hear and heal when his people “humble themselves, pray, seek my face”, is often quoted. It was first spoken to Israel about the temple, and Christians differ on how directly to apply it to a modern nation or church.

The book’s wider theme is widely shared: it is never too late to turn back to God.

Solomon begins his reign with a crowd and a sacrifice. He leads all Israel to the high place at Gibeon, where the old Tent of Meeting that Moses made still stands with the bronze altar, and he offers a thousand burnt offerings. That night God appears to him with an open invitation: “Ask for what you want me to give you.” Solomon begins by remembering the kindness shown to his father David. Then he asks for wisdom and knowledge to govern a people as many as the dust of the earth. God is pleased that he did not ask for riches, honor, or the death of his enemies, and grants the wisdom, adding wealth and honor beyond any king before or after. Solomon returns to Jerusalem and reigns. The chapter closes with chariots, horsemen, and so much silver and gold that they are as common as stones.

The scene is also in 1 Kings 3. Chronicles places it at Gibeon because the tent and altar of Moses were there while David's tent for the ark stood in Jerusalem, as chapter 21 of the first book said. Solomon's request fits what David asked of him in 1 Chronicles 22. The horses from Egypt in verse 16 may be read alongside the warning about kings in Deuteronomy 17. The book is usually dated after the exile.

Solomon decides to build, and the planning is as important as the building. He counts out seventy thousand burden bearers, eighty thousand stone cutters in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred overseers. Then he writes to Huram, king of Tyre, and asks for the same help Tyre once gave David: cedar, cypress, skilled metalworkers, and men who can cut timber in Lebanon. In return he will send wheat, barley, wine and oil. He explains his own thinking with some humility, saying, “heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain him”, and asks who he is to build God a house, except to burn incense before him. Huram answers in writing with a blessing for the LORD, who made heaven and earth, and he sends Huram-abi, a skilled man whose mother was from Dan and whose father was from Tyre. Solomon puts the foreigners in the land to the work.

The exchange of letters appears in 1 Kings 5, in a shorter form. Huram is called Hiram there. The workforce was drawn from the foreigners living in Israel, counted in a census after the one David took, and readers rightly ask about the fairness of such forced labor, which the text reports without comment. Many scholars think Chronicles was shaped after the exile.

The chapter opens with a place: Solomon begins to build on Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. The date is given too, the second day of the second month in the fourth year of his reign. After that the text reads like a builder's account. The house is sixty cubits long and twenty wide. The porch is overlaid with pure gold, the large room is paneled with cypress and fine gold, and carved palm trees and chains decorate it. The most holy place is twenty cubits square, overlaid with six hundred talents of fine gold. Two carved cherubim stand there, their wings reaching twenty cubits in all, and a veil of blue, purple, crimson and fine linen hangs before them. Outside, two bronze pillars stand, one on the right named Jachin and one on the left named Boaz.

The threshing floor links this chapter to 1 Chronicles 21. Mount Moriah is also the name used for the land where Abraham went in Genesis 22, and tradition has long connected the two, though the text here does not say so. The description parallels 1 Kings 6 and 7. The cubit measures and the weights of gold should be taken as the writer gives them. Many scholars date Chronicles after the exile.

The furnishings follow the house. Solomon makes a bronze altar twenty cubits square. Then he casts the molten sea, a huge round basin ten cubits across, resting on twelve bronze oxen that face north, west, south and east, with a rim like the flower of a lily. It holds three thousand baths and is for the priests to wash in. He makes ten basins for the offerings, ten golden lamp stands and ten tables, a hundred golden basins, and a court for the priests with doors overlaid in bronze. The craftsman Huram-abi, whose work is credited to him, makes the pots, shovels and bowls, and the two pillars with their networks and four hundred pomegranates. The metal was cast in the plain of the Jordan, between Succoth and Zeredah, and there was so much bronze that its weight was never worked out. The chapter ends with the golden altar and the table for the bread.

The washing basins echo the tabernacle of Exodus 30 and 38. Chronicles parallels 1 Kings 7 here and describes the temple as built to continue the worship begun in the wilderness, with more of everything. Some details, such as the size of the sea, are discussed by readers because the measurements are rounded. Many scholars think the book was written after the exile for people rebuilding worship.

The work is done, and Solomon brings in what David had dedicated, the silver, gold and vessels, and puts them in the treasuries. Then he summons Israel to Jerusalem. In the seventh month, at the feast, the elders gather and the Levites take up the ark and bring it into the inner sanctuary, under the wings of the cherubim. So many sheep and cattle are sacrificed that they cannot be counted. The poles of the ark are so long their ends can be seen from the holy place. The text says nothing is in the ark except the two tablets Moses put there at Horeb. The priests come out, the singers stand at the east end of the altar in fine linen, with a hundred twenty priests blowing trumpets. They are as one voice, saying, “For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever”. Then a cloud fills the house, so that the priests cannot stand to minister, for the glory of the LORD fills it.

This is the dedication scene, also in 1 Kings 8. A cloud as a sign of God's presence recalls the tabernacle in Exodus 40 and the pillar of cloud in the wilderness. The words of praise are a refrain in this book and in the Psalms (see Psalm 136). Many scholars think Chronicles was written after the exile, for a community that needed to know that God's presence did not depend on a king.

The cloud has filled the house, and Solomon speaks into it. The LORD has said he would dwell in thick darkness, he says, and I have built you a house. He turns and blesses the assembly, then recalls the promise to David, who wanted to build but was told his son would. Then he kneels on a bronze platform in the court, spreads his hands to heaven, and prays. He asks God to keep the promise to David's line. Then he asks the question that sits in the middle of the chapter: “But will God indeed dwell with men on the earth?” Heaven cannot contain God, much less this house. Yet he asks that God's eyes be open toward it. A long run of cases follows: a wrong between neighbors, defeat in war, drought, famine, plague, a foreigner who comes from far away, and exile. In each, he asks God to hear from heaven and forgive.

This prayer parallels 1 Kings 8 and is one of the great prayers of the Bible. Its mention of exile in verses 36 to 39 is striking, since many scholars think the book was written after the exile began and ended. Note the foreigner in verse 32, for whom Solomon asks that God answer so that all peoples may know his name. Readers differ on how the house relates to God's presence, a question the New Testament takes up in places such as Acts 7.

Solomon has finished praying, and the answer is immediate. Fire comes down from heaven and consumes the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD fills the house so completely that the priests cannot enter. All Israel sees it. They bow with their faces to the ground, worship, and give thanks. Then the king and the people offer sacrifices, twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred twenty thousand sheep, and the dedication lasts seven days, followed by the feast, then a solemn assembly. On the twenty-third day Solomon sends the people home, joyful and glad of heart. Then God appears to him by night. He has heard the prayer and chosen the place. Then comes a promise that is often quoted: if his people humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn from wicked ways, he will hear from heaven, forgive, and “will heal their land.” A warning follows, that if they forsake him, the house itself will become a byword.

The promise in verse 14 was given to Israel at a particular time and place, and readers differ on how far it applies to other nations and eras. The fire from heaven echoes Leviticus 9 and 1 Kings 18. The warning in verses 19 to 22 looks ahead to the fall of Jerusalem, a story told at the end of this book. Many scholars think Chronicles was written after the exile and for people who had lived through it.

Twenty years of building are over, and the king looks around at what he has made. The temple stands, and so does his own house. Now Solomon turns to the rest of his kingdom. He rebuilds the cities Huram gave him and settles Israelites in them. He wins a victory at Hamath Zobah, builds Tadmor in the wilderness, fortifies the two Beth Horons with walls, gates and bars, and fills storage cities and chariot cities across his land.

The chapter is honest about who carried the weight. The people left over from the old nations of Canaan were conscripted for forced labor, while the Israelites served as soldiers and officers, two hundred fifty chief officers in all. Solomon also moves Pharaoh’s daughter out of David’s city, because “the places where the LORD’s ark has come are holy.” His offerings follow the rhythm of the law of Moses, and the priests and Levites serve in the divisions David set. Then the ships sail, and gold comes back from Ophir.

Chronicles tells Solomon’s reign with the temple at its center, and here the temple is finished and its worship is running. Huram, who supplied help for the building earlier (see 2 Chronicles 2), now supplies ships and sailors. The chapter shows a king who builds widely and keeps worship in order, and it also records forced labor without comment, a hard fact to read. The story continues in chapter 9 with the visitors who come to see Solomon.

A rumor travels far. The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon’s fame and decides to test it for herself, so she comes to Jerusalem with a very great caravan of camels, spices, gold and precious stones. She brings hard questions and talks with him about all that is in her heart. He answers every one. Then she sees the house he built, the food on his table, his servants and ministers, and the way he goes up to the LORD’s house, and there is no more spirit in her.

She admits she did not believe the reports until her own eyes saw. Half the greatness of his wisdom, she says, was never told her. She blesses the LORD his God, gives gifts, and goes home with all she asked for. The rest of the chapter counts his wealth: gold by the talent, shields of beaten gold, an ivory throne with twelve lions on its steps, ships bringing apes and peacocks, and kings who come to hear him. Forty years pass, Solomon dies, and Rehoboam takes his place.

This is the high point of Solomon’s reign in Chronicles. The visit of the queen of Sheba is also told in 1 Kings 10, and Chronicles keeps its focus on the wisdom God gave him and on her words of praise to the LORD. Wealth and fame are at their peak here. The next chapter shows how quickly the kingdom divides once the son takes the throne.

Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has gathered to make him king. Jeroboam, who fled to Egypt from Solomon, comes back and speaks for the people. Their request is simple: ease the heavy service your father laid on us, and we will serve you. Rehoboam asks for three days.

He asks the old men who stood before Solomon, and they tell him to be kind and speak good words. He sets that aside and asks the young men he grew up with. They tell him to say that his little finger is thicker than his father’s waist, and that he will add to the yoke. On the third day the king answers roughly, and the people give their answer: “Every man to your tents, Israel!” Rehoboam sends Hadoram, who is over the forced labor, and the people stone him. The king flees to Jerusalem, and Israel breaks away from David’s house.

Solomon’s long reign ended with heavy demands on the people (see 2 Chronicles 8 and 9). Rehoboam is his son, crowned at Shechem in the north. The writer says the outcome was brought about by God to establish the word spoken through Ahijah to Jeroboam, and the chapter still shows a king who chose a harsh answer. The kingdom now has two parts, Israel in the north and Judah in the south.

Rehoboam comes home to Jerusalem with a plan for war. He gathers one hundred eighty thousand chosen men from Judah and Benjamin to take back the north. Then a word comes through Shemaiah, a man of God, and the plan stops. They are not to fight their brothers, because this thing is of the LORD. The army listens and goes home.

Rehoboam turns to defense instead. He fortifies fifteen cities, from Bethlehem and Tekoa to Lachish and Hebron, and stocks them with food, oil, wine, shields and spears. Meanwhile Jeroboam has cast out the priests and Levites and made his own priests for the high places and the calf idols. The Levites leave their pasture lands and come to Judah, and so do many from every tribe who set their hearts to seek the LORD. For three years they strengthen Rehoboam’s kingdom. The chapter ends in his family: wives, concubines, many sons and daughters, and Abijah named as chief among his brothers.

The kingdom has just split (see 2 Chronicles 10). The chapter shows Judah choosing not to fight and then preparing to survive. Chronicles pays close attention to the temple and its priests, so the move of the Levites to Judah matters to the writer. The big family at the end shows a king who is secure, which is the setting for what goes wrong in chapter 12.

Strength is a test, and Rehoboam fails it. Once his kingdom is established and he is strong, he leaves the LORD’s law, and all Israel goes with him. In the fifth year Shishak king of Egypt comes up against Jerusalem with twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen and a people without number. He takes the fortified cities of Judah.

Then Shemaiah the prophet finds the king and the princes gathered in Jerusalem. His message is hard: “You have forsaken me, therefore I have also left you in the hand of Shishak.” The leaders humble themselves and say, “The LORD is righteous.” God sees it and grants some deliverance, though they will serve Shishak. Shishak takes the treasures of both houses, including the golden shields of Solomon. Rehoboam replaces them with bronze ones, and a guard carries them whenever he enters the temple. The chapter closes with a verdict that is mixed: because he humbled himself, he was not destroyed, yet he did evil, because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.

Rehoboam reigned seventeen years, according to the chapter. Shishak is the Egyptian king of that time, and 1 Kings 14 also records his attack. Chronicles uses the story to show a pattern: leaving God brings trouble, and humbling oneself brings relief. The bronze shields standing in for gold make the point in a concrete way.

Two armies face each other, and one is outnumbered two to one. Abijah of Judah has four hundred thousand chosen men, and Jeroboam brings eight hundred thousand. Before the fighting begins, Abijah climbs Mount Zemaraim and calls across to Israel. He reminds them that the LORD gave the kingdom to David and his sons by a covenant of salt. He says Jeroboam rebelled, that Israel carries golden calves, and that Jeroboam drove out the priests of the LORD. Judah, he says, still keeps the daily offerings and the lamp stand.

Jeroboam sends an ambush behind Judah, so the battle is before and behind them. Judah cries to the LORD, the priests sound the trumpets, and the men shout. God strikes Jeroboam and all Israel, and five hundred thousand of Israel’s chosen men fall. The writer gives the reason: Judah prevailed “because they relied on the LORD”. Abijah takes Bethel and two other towns, and Jeroboam never recovers his strength.

Abijah is Rehoboam’s son and reigns three years. His speech is a statement of Judah’s case: the David line, the temple priests and the right worship. Many readers note that the same king is judged less kindly in 1 Kings 15, and Chronicles gives this chapter a more favorable picture. The large numbers are as the text gives them. Chapter 14 begins with his death and his son Asa.

After the war comes quiet, and quiet gives Asa the chance to build. His father Abijah has died, and for ten years the land has rest. Asa does what is good and right in the LORD’s eyes. He takes away the foreign altars and high places, breaks the pillars and cuts down the Asherah poles, and tells Judah to seek the LORD. He builds fortified cities and says that the land is theirs because they have sought the LORD, who has given them rest on every side.

Then rest ends. Zerah the Ethiopian comes with an army of a million troops and three hundred chariots, and he reaches Mareshah. Asa has a large army too, but he does not trust it. He cries to the LORD: “LORD, you are our God.” In his prayer, he says that there is no one besides the LORD to help the mighty or the weak. The LORD strikes the Ethiopians, and they flee. Judah pursues them to Gerar, plunders the cities, and returns to Jerusalem with sheep and camels in abundance.

Asa is the third king of Judah after the split, and Chronicles gives him a long and mostly good reign. The chapter shows peace and then a threat, and it shows what Asa does when he is outnumbered. His prayer here is worth comparing with what he does later in chapter 16.

A prophet meets a king on the road home from victory. The Spirit of God comes on Azariah the son of Oded, and he tells Asa and all Judah a rule that sounds like a proverb: “The LORD is with you while you are with him”. If they seek him, he will be found. If they forsake him, he will forsake them. Azariah looks back at hard times when Israel turned to God in distress and found him. Then he tells the king to be strong, for the work will be rewarded.

Asa takes courage. He removes the abominations from the land and renews the altar. In the third month of the fifteenth year, crowds gather in Jerusalem, many from the north, and they offer seven hundred cattle and seven thousand sheep. They enter a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart and swear it with shouting and trumpets. The text records that anyone who would not seek him was to be put to death. Asa even removes his own mother from her place as queen mother for making an image of Asherah.

Asa has just returned from the battle in chapter 14. The speech by Azariah is a short sermon on the main idea of Chronicles, that God answers those who seek him. The oath with its death penalty is hard to read today, and the text says only what the assembly swore. The high places were still not taken away out of Israel, which the writer notes beside the king’s whole heart.

The chapter opens in the thirty-sixth year, and it shows a different Asa. Baasha king of Israel builds Ramah to cut Judah off. Asa takes silver and gold from the LORD’s house and the king’s house and sends it to Ben Hadad of Syria, asking him to break his treaty with Baasha. It works. Syria strikes Israel’s cities, Baasha stops building, and Asa carries away the stones and timber of Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah.

Then Hanani the seer comes with a rebuke. Asa relied on the king of Syria and not on the LORD, who gave him the huge Ethiopian army. “the LORD’s eyes run back and forth throughout the whole earth” to show himself strong for those whose heart is perfect toward him, Hanani says, and from now on Asa will have wars. Asa is angry, puts the seer in prison, and oppresses some of the people. In the thirty-ninth year his feet are diseased, and in his illness he seeks the physicians and not the LORD. He dies in the forty-first year and is buried in his own tomb.

In chapter 14 Asa cried to God against a million men, and here he trusts a treaty against a smaller threat. The writer sets the two scenes side by side. The comment about physicians has been read in different ways: many readers take it as a note about his heart and not as a rule about medicine. Nothing in the chapter gives medical advice.

Jehoshaphat begins by strengthening Judah. He puts forces in the fortified cities and garrisons in the land. The LORD is with him, because he walked in the first ways of David his father and did not seek the Baals. His kingdom is established, and tribute and riches pour in. The writer says his heart was lifted up in the ways of the LORD, and he took away the high places and Asherah poles.

Then comes something quieter and unusual. In the third year of his reign he sends his princes, with Levites and priests, to teach in the cities of Judah. They carry the book of the LORD’s law with them and go through all the cities, teaching the people. The fear of the LORD falls on the nations around, so that no one makes war on him. Philistines bring presents, and Arabians bring flocks. Jehoshaphat builds fortresses and store cities, and the chapter ends with a long list of his captains and their armies, in the hundreds of thousands, from Judah and Benjamin.

Jehoshaphat is Asa’s son and reigns twenty-five years (see 2 Chronicles 20). Chronicles likes to tell what a king did for worship and teaching. This chapter is the high point of his early reign, and the numbers of soldiers show how secure the kingdom was. The next chapter shows what happens when he joins himself to the house of Ahab.

Jehoshaphat has riches and honor in abundance, and he does something that will cost him: he allies himself with Ahab, king of Israel. In Samaria, Ahab kills sheep and cattle for him and persuades him to go up to Ramoth Gilead. Jehoshaphat says he is with him, but he asks first for the LORD’s word. Four hundred prophets say, “Go up”. Zedekiah even makes horns of iron. Jehoshaphat is not satisfied and asks if there is another prophet.

There is one, Micaiah, and Ahab hates him because he never says anything good about him. A messenger tells him to join the others. At first Micaiah repeats their words. Pressed for the truth, he describes Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd. Then he describes the LORD on his throne and a lying spirit in the mouths of the prophets. Zedekiah strikes him, and Ahab has him put in prison. In battle Ahab disguises himself, but an arrow shot at random strikes him between the joints of his armor, and he dies at sunset. Jehoshaphat cries out, and the LORD helps him.

This is the story also told in 1 Kings 22. Micaiah’s vision of the heavenly court is a difficult passage, and readers differ on how to understand the lying spirit. The text says God permits it as a judgment on Ahab. The main contrast is between four hundred voices that please the king and one voice that tells the truth. Ahab’s alliance with Judah began through marriage (see 2 Chronicles 21).

Jehoshaphat comes home in peace, but he does not come home unchallenged. Jehu the son of Hanani meets him with a question that stings: “Should you help the wicked, and love those who hate the LORD?” There is wrath on him for this. Yet Jehu also names what is good in him, that he put away the Asheroth and set his heart to seek God.

The king answers by going back to work. He goes out among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and brings them back to the LORD. Then he appoints judges in every fortified city of Judah, and he gives them a charge. They do not judge for man but for the LORD, and the LORD is with them in the judgment. There is no injustice with the LORD, no favoritism and no bribe. In Jerusalem he sets up a higher court of Levites, priests and heads of families, with Amariah the chief priest over matters of the LORD and Zebadiah over the king’s matters. His last word to them is “Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the good.”

Jehu the son of Hanani is the son of the Hanani who rebuked Asa in chapter 16. Jehoshaphat’s reform of the courts is one of the best-known acts of his reign. The charge to the judges is short and plain, and it ties fair judging to the character of God. It follows his mistake in chapter 18, so the chapter shows a king who is corrected and then acts.

The bad news comes from far away. A great multitude from Moab, Ammon and beyond is coming, and they are already at En Gedi. Jehoshaphat is alarmed, and what he does with his alarm is the heart of the chapter. He sets himself to seek the LORD and calls a fast for all Judah. In the temple court he prays, naming God’s power and the land given to Abraham’s offspring, and he ends with honest words: “We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”

The whole assembly stands there, with little ones, wives and children. The Spirit comes on Jahaziel, a Levite, who tells them not to be afraid, because the battle is God’s. The next morning Jehoshaphat appoints singers to go before the army, saying, “Give thanks to the LORD”. When they begin to sing, the enemy turns on itself, and none escape. Judah gathers plunder for three days, blesses the LORD in the Valley of Beracah, and returns to Jerusalem with harps and trumpets. The chapter ends with a sad note about Jehoshaphat’s ships, which were wrecked.

This is the best-known story of Jehoshaphat. The prayer is a model of how Chronicles pictures prayer at the temple (see 1 Kings 8 and 2 Chronicles 6). The order of events is unusual: worship goes ahead of the army. The closing verses show that even a good king made mistakes, and the shipwreck is tied to his alliance with Ahaziah of Israel.

A father leaves gifts to his sons, but the kingdom goes to one. Jehoshaphat dies, and his firstborn Jehoram takes the throne. As soon as he is strong, he kills all his brothers with the sword, and some of the princes too. He walks in the way of the kings of Israel, as Ahab’s house did, because Ahab’s daughter is his wife. Yet the LORD would not destroy David’s house, because of the covenant he made with David.

The rest of the chapter is a slow collapse. Edom revolts, and Libnah too. Jehoram builds high places and leads Judah astray. A letter comes from Elijah the prophet, naming his crimes, including the brothers he killed who were better than himself, and warning of a plague and a terrible illness. The Philistines and Arabians break into Judah and carry off his possessions, his wives and all his sons but the youngest. Jehoram dies after two years of sickness. He “departed with no one’s regret”, and he is buried in David’s city but not in the tombs of the kings.

Jehoram reigns eight years. The marriage to Ahab’s daughter is the turning point, because it brought the worship and politics of the northern royal house into Judah. The letter from Elijah is unusual, since the stories about Elijah elsewhere are set in the north (see 1 Kings 17 and following). The chapter is hard reading, and it stresses that God keeps his promise to David even as this king fails.

One death after another empties the throne of Judah. After the Arabians kill the older sons, the people of Jerusalem make Ahaziah, the youngest, king. His mother is Athaliah, a daughter of Omri, and she is his counselor in doing wrong. He follows Ahab’s house into war against Hazael of Syria at Ramoth Gilead, and then he goes to Jezreel to see the wounded Jehoram of Israel. There he meets Jehu, whom the LORD anointed to cut off Ahab’s house. Jehu kills the princes of Judah who serve Ahaziah and then Ahaziah himself, who is hiding in Samaria. He is buried because he is the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart.

Then the darkest moment: Athaliah sees that her son is dead, and she destroys all the royal offspring of Judah. But Jehoshabeath, the king’s daughter and the wife of Jehoiada the priest, takes Joash, Ahaziah’s infant son, from among the king’s sons who were being killed. She hides him with his nurse. For six years, he stays hidden in God’s house while Athaliah rules the land.

The line of David seems to be down to a child. The chapter ties together the families of Judah and Israel through marriage. The story of Jehu’s purge in the north is told in 2 Kings 9 and 10. In Chronicles the writer treats the end of Ahaziah as God’s doing. The hope of the chapter is small and quiet: one baby hidden in the temple.

For six years a boy hides in the temple, and then a priest decides it is time. In the seventh year, Jehoiada makes a covenant with five captains of hundreds. They gather the Levites and the heads of families from the cities of Judah, and the whole assembly makes a covenant with the young king in God’s house. Jehoiada says the king’s son must reign, as the LORD spoke about the sons of David.

He plans it carefully, with guards at the thresholds and gates and the Levites around the king with weapons. He hands out the spears and shields that were David’s. Then they bring out the king’s son, crown him, give him the covenant and anoint him. “Long live the king!” they shout. Athaliah hears the noise, comes into the temple, tears her clothes and cries, “Treason! treason!” Jehoiada orders that she not be killed in the LORD’s house, and she is killed at the horse gate. Jehoiada makes a covenant that they should be the LORD’s people, and the people tear down the house of Baal. The city is quiet.

This is the other half of the story in chapter 22, and it is also told in 2 Kings 11. The chapter shows how much power sat with the priest, who led the revolt and renewed the covenant. Joash is still a child. Readers may notice that the writer is careful about holiness: no one unclean was to enter, and the queen was not to be killed in the LORD’s house.

Joash is seven years old when he begins to reign, and while Jehoiada lives he does what is right. When he grows up, he decides to restore the LORD’s house, which the sons of Athaliah had broken up. The Levites are slow, so the king orders a chest to be placed outside the gate of the LORD’s house. People rejoice and fill it, again and again, and the money pays masons, carpenters and metalworkers.

Then Jehoiada dies, one hundred thirty years old. After his death, the princes of Judah bow to the king, and he listens to them. They abandon the house of the LORD and serve idols. Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada, speaks, and by the king’s command he is stoned in the court of the LORD’s house. As he dies he says, “May the LORD look at it, and repay it.” Within a year the Syrians come, and Joash is badly wounded. His own servants kill him in his bed, and he is not buried in the tombs of the kings.

Joash is the child saved in chapters 22 and 23. The first half of his reign shows what a good counselor can do, and the second half shows what happens without one. The text names the kindness of Jehoiada as the very thing the king forgot. Jesus refers to the blood of a Zechariah killed in the temple area in Matthew 23, and readers differ on whether this is the same person.

Amaziah begins well and does only half of what is right: the text says he did what was right in the LORD’s eyes, but not with a perfect heart. When he is secure, he executes the servants who killed his father, but he spares their children, as the law of Moses says each person dies for his own sin. He hires a hundred thousand men from Israel for a hundred talents of silver.

A man of God tells him not to take Israel’s army. Amaziah asks about the silver, and is told the LORD can give him much more. He sends the hired men home, and they return in a fury. He wins a victory in the Valley of Salt, and then he brings home the gods of Seir and bows to them. A prophet questions him, but the king silences him. Amaziah then challenges Joash of Israel, who answers with a story about a thistle and a cedar. They fight at Beth Shemesh, and Judah is defeated. In the end a conspiracy forms against Amaziah, and he is killed at Lachish.

Amaziah is the son of Joash from chapter 24. The text quotes from Deuteronomy 24 when it explains why he spared the children. The chapter includes the killing of captured Edomites (verse 12), which is stated plainly, and the writer does not comment on it. The central contrast is between a king who obeys some commands and a king whose pride leads him into a needless war.

Uzziah is sixteen when the people make him king, and he reigns fifty-two years. He seeks God in the days of Zechariah, and as long as he seeks the LORD, God makes him prosper. He breaks the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod, and the Ammonites pay tribute. He builds towers and cisterns and loves farming. His army is more than three hundred thousand, and skilled men make devices for shooting arrows and great stones from the towers. His name spreads to the border of Egypt, because he was “marvelously helped until he was strong”.

Then the strong king crosses a line. His heart is lifted up, and he goes into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense, a task for the priests. Azariah the priest and eighty others stand in his way. Uzziah is angry, and leprosy breaks out on his forehead. They hurry him out, and he hurries too. He lives in a separate house until he dies, and his son Jotham runs the household.

Uzziah is also called Azariah in 2 Kings 15. His reign is long, and Isaiah 6 begins in the year he died. The chapter shows a conflict between royal power and priestly duty, as the law of Moses reserved the incense to the sons of Aaron (see Exodus 30 and Numbers 16). The word translated leprosy covers several skin conditions in the Bible.

After a king who grew proud, here is a king who is steady. Jotham is twenty-five when he begins to reign, and he reigns sixteen years. His mother is Jerushah, a daughter of Zadok. He does what is right in the LORD’s eyes, as his father Uzziah did, with one difference: he does not enter the LORD’s temple. The people, meanwhile, still act corruptly.

He builds the upper gate of the LORD’s house and works much on the wall of Ophel. He builds cities in the hill country and fortresses and towers in the forests. He fights the king of the Ammonites and prevails, and for three years the Ammonites give him a hundred talents of silver and ten thousand cors each of wheat and barley. The writer gives the reason for his strength in a single line: “Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God.” The chapter ends quickly. His other acts are in the book of the kings, and after he dies and is buried in David’s city, his son Ahaz reigns.

This is the shortest of the reigns in this part of Chronicles, and it has no failure to report against the king. It is also a hinge between Uzziah and Ahaz, whose reign in chapter 28 goes in a very different direction. The remark about the temple is usually read as a lesson from his father’s case, though the text does not say so.

Ahaz is twenty, and he does not do what David did. He makes images for the Baals and burns incense in the valley of Hinnom. The text says he burned his children in the fire. Judah pays for it. Syria carries off captives to Damascus, and Pekah of Israel kills a hundred twenty thousand in one day. Israel takes two hundred thousand women and children captive and brings them toward Samaria.

A prophet named Oded stops the army. He tells them that God gave Judah into their hands in anger, but that they have their own guilt too, and the captives must go back. Some leaders of Ephraim agree. They take the captives, clothe those who were naked, give them sandals, food and drink, put the feeble on donkeys, and bring them to Jericho. It is the one bright moment of the chapter. Ahaz sends to Assyria, but it does not help him. He sacrifices to the gods of Damascus because they had defeated him. He cuts up the vessels of God’s house and shuts its doors. When he dies, he is not placed in the tombs of the kings.

Ahaz was a king of Judah in the time of the prophet Isaiah, and Isaiah 7 tells of his meeting with the prophet. The sacrifice of children by fire is condemned in the law (see Leviticus 18 and Deuteronomy 18). Oded’s speech is notable because a prophet of the LORD in the north defends people from the south. Hezekiah follows in the next chapter.

A new king opens the doors. Hezekiah is twenty-five when he begins to reign, and in the first month of his first year he opens the doors of the LORD’s house and repairs them. He gathers the priests and Levites and tells them to sanctify themselves and carry the filthiness out of the holy place. He names the cause of Judah’s troubles: their fathers were unfaithful, shut the doors, put out the lamps and stopped the offerings. Now it is in his heart to make a covenant with the LORD.

The Levites rise and do the work. They cleanse the temple in sixteen days and report that the altar and the vessels Ahaz threw away are ready. Hezekiah brings seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs and seven male goats as a sin offering for the kingdom. When the burnt offering begins, the song of the LORD begins too, with the trumpets and instruments of David. All the assembly worships. Then the people bring so many offerings that the priests are too few, and the Levites help. The chapter ends with joy, because the thing was done suddenly.

Hezekiah reigns twenty-nine years, and his reforms take up chapters 29 to 31. Chapter 28 ended with the temple shut, so this chapter starts with the doors. The details of the offerings and the music match the arrangements of David (see 1 Chronicles 23 to 25). The scene is one of repentance and restoring worship before any other project.

A king writes letters to a divided people. Hezekiah wants to keep the Passover in Jerusalem, and he invites all Israel and Judah, including Ephraim and Manasseh in the north. They cannot keep it at the usual time, so they decide on the second month. Couriers carry the invitation from Beersheba to Dan: turn again to the LORD, and he will return to the remnant that escaped the kings of Assyria. The couriers promise that he is “gracious and merciful”.

In many towns people mock the couriers. But some from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humble themselves and come, and in Judah God gives one heart. A very great assembly gathers and removes the altars of Jerusalem. Many who come are not clean, and they eat the Passover in a way other than what is written. Hezekiah prays for them, asking that the good LORD pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God. The LORD listens and heals the people. They keep the feast seven days, then agree to keep another seven. The writer says that since Solomon there was nothing like this joy in Jerusalem.

The northern kingdom has fallen to Assyria, or is about to, depending on the timing, and the letters are addressed to those who remain. The Passover is held a month late, which the law allows in some cases (see Numbers 9). The prayer for the unclean is a notable moment: the chapter puts a sincere heart before strict form, and the LORD answers it.

When the feast is over, the people do something on their own. They go out to the cities of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh and break the pillars, cut down the Asherah poles and tear down the high places and altars. Then they go home.

Hezekiah sets the priests and Levites in their divisions and gives the king’s portion for the daily and festival offerings, as written in the law. He commands the people in Jerusalem to give the portion for the priests and Levites, so that they can give themselves to the LORD’s law. The response is fast and large. People bring first fruits of grain, wine, oil and honey, and the tithe of everything, and they pile it in heaps. When Hezekiah and the princes see the heaps, they bless the LORD. Azariah the chief priest says they have “eaten and had enough”, with plenty left over. Hezekiah has rooms prepared in the temple, appoints overseers, and arranges distribution by name and by division. The chapter ends with the verdict that he did what was good, right and faithful, and prospered.

This chapter shows the practical side of a reform: after repairs and a festival, the priests and Levites need to be supported. The command about portions rests on the law of Moses (see Numbers 18). Giving here is described as generous and willing, and the surplus is the result. The next chapter shows that faithfulness does not spare Hezekiah a crisis.

The chapter begins with a hard phrase: after all this faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria comes. He camps against the fortified cities, and Hezekiah sees that he means to fight against Jerusalem. The king prepares. He and his leaders stop the springs outside the city, repair the wall, and make weapons. Then he gathers the people at the city gate and says, “Be strong and courageous.” An arm of flesh is with Sennacherib, but the LORD is with them.

Sennacherib’s servants come with mocking words. They say no god of any nation could save its people, so how could Hezekiah’s God? They shout in the language of the Jews to frighten the people on the wall. Hezekiah and Isaiah the prophet pray and cry to heaven. The LORD sends an angel who cuts off the mighty men, leaders and captains in the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib goes home in shame, and his own sons kill him in the house of his god. Hezekiah’s story ends more mixed. He is terminally ill and prays. His heart is lifted up, and wrath comes, but he humbles himself. He is honored at his death.

This siege is also told in 2 Kings 18 to 20 and in Isaiah 36 to 39. Assyrian records of Sennacherib’s campaign have survived, and many historians use them with the Bible. The water tunnel hinted at in verse 30 is usually linked by scholars with the Siloam tunnel in Jerusalem. The chapter is brief about the visit from Babylon, which comes back later (see 2 Kings 20).

The longest reign in Judah’s history begins with a child. Manasseh is twelve years old, and he reigns fifty-five years. He rebuilds the high places his father broke down, raises altars for the Baals, and worships the army of the sky. He builds altars in the two courts of the LORD’s house. He makes his children pass through the fire, practices sorcery, and sets an idol in God’s house, the place where God had said his name would be forever. The LORD speaks to Manasseh and his people, but they do not listen.

Then the Assyrian captains take Manasseh in chains to Babylon. In distress, he begs the LORD and humbles himself greatly. God hears him and brings him back to Jerusalem. “Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.” He builds an outer wall, removes the foreign gods and the idol from the temple, and restores the altar. His son Amon returns to the idols and does not humble himself. His servants kill him in his house, and the people of the land make his son Josiah king.

This chapter is parallel to 2 Kings 21, but Chronicles alone tells of Manasseh’s exile and return. Many scholars see this as the writer’s way of showing that repentance is always possible. The text mentions his prayer in verse 18, and a later prayer under his name exists outside the Bible, although it is not part of the World English Bible. The people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD.

Josiah is eight years old when he becomes king, and the story comes in steps. In the eighth year he begins to seek the God of David, while still young. In the twelfth year he begins to purge Judah and Jerusalem of high places, Asherah poles and images, and he goes into the northern cities too.

In the eighteenth year, he sends men to repair the LORD’s house. While they handle the money, Hilkiah the priest finds the book of the LORD’s law given by Moses. Shaphan the scribe reads it to the king, who tears his clothes. He sends a delegation to Huldah the prophetess. Her message has two parts: evil will come on this place because the people forsook the LORD, but the king, whose heart was tender and who humbled himself, will be gathered to his grave in peace and will not see it. Josiah gathers the elders, reads the whole book of the covenant to the people in the LORD’s house, and makes a covenant to walk after the LORD with all his heart. All his days, the people do not depart from the LORD.

Josiah reigns thirty-one years, and the same events are told in 2 Kings 22 and 23. Many scholars think the book found in the temple was all or part of Deuteronomy, though the text only calls it the book of the law. Huldah is one of the few women named as a prophet in Scripture (see also Exodus 15, Judges 4). The order of events differs a little from 2 Kings.

Josiah keeps a Passover that is remembered for generations. He sets the priests in their offices and tells the Levites to put the holy ark in the house Solomon built, since it will no longer be a burden on their shoulders. He gives thirty thousand lambs and young goats and three thousand bulls from his own possessions, and his princes give more. The Levites kill the lambs, the priests sprinkle the blood, and the offerings are carried quickly to all the people. The singers and gatekeepers stay at their posts, because the Levites prepare for them. The writer says there was no Passover like it since the days of Samuel.

Then the chapter turns. Neco king of Egypt goes up to fight at Carchemish. Josiah goes out against him, and Neco sends word that his quarrel is not with Judah and that God has commanded him to hurry. Josiah will not turn back, disguises himself, and goes to the valley of Megiddo. Archers shoot him. He dies in Jerusalem, and all Judah mourns, and Jeremiah laments for him.

This chapter is the end of the good kings in Judah. It parallels 2 Kings 23, although the death of Josiah is told differently. The text says Neco spoke from the mouth of God, and readers have read that in different ways. The Passover details follow the law of Moses (see Exodus 12 and Deuteronomy 16). The final chapter shows how quickly the kingdom ends.

The last chapter of the book moves fast. After Josiah, the people make Jehoahaz king, but the king of Egypt removes him after three months and sets his brother Eliakim on the throne, renamed Jehoiakim. Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon binds Jehoiakim in fetters and takes some of the temple vessels to Babylon. Jehoiachin, eight years old, reigns three months before he is taken to Babylon too. Then Zedekiah is made king. He does evil, will not humble himself before Jeremiah, and rebels against the king of Babylon.

The writer gives the cause: the priests and the people copied the abominations of the nations. God sent messengers again and again out of compassion, but they mocked them, until there was no remedy. The Chaldeans burn God’s house, break down Jerusalem’s wall, and carry the survivors to Babylon. The land lies desolate for seventy years. Then, in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, the LORD stirs the king’s spirit, and Cyrus announces that God has told him to build a house in Jerusalem. “Whoever there is among you of all his people”, he says, may go up.

Chronicles ends here, and its last two verses are nearly the same as the opening of the book of Ezra. In the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles comes last, so the story ends with an open door. The seventy years refer to Jeremiah (see Jeremiah 25 and 29). The chapter is a hard account of the fall of Jerusalem, and it still closes with a call to go home.
